answer.rationale: Three concurrent signals point to the release as the proximate cause of the write-path latency climb: the release deployed 2 hours ago and p99 has been climbing for 90 minutes, a tight causal window. The primary objective—maximize sustained availability without losing customer writes—favors the intervention most likely to restore write-path latency to target while preserving the existing settlement traffic. A rollback to the prior stable build restores write-path health immediately; settlement writes continue to be processed (they were before the release and will continue on the prior build), and no customer writes are lost because the rollback reverts code, not data. Regional failover (memory_b2) addresses infrastructure degradation, but the latency climb correlates with the release, not a regional event. Adding capacity (memory_b3) helps absorb demand, but the problem is not queue depth—it is write-path latency degrading 5x, suggesting a code-level regression rather than insufficient headroom. Enabling a circuit breaker (memory_b4) contains a downstream partner outage; there is no indication of a partner dependency failing here. Routing reads to replicas (memory_b5) relieves primary load from dashboard queries, but the problem is explicitly on the write path, not read replicas. Memory_b1 is the closest analog: a release caused an error spike, rollback to the prior stable build cleared it without customer impact. Verifying memory_b1 confirms the rollback completed cleanly and the prior build was stable, which directly supports confidence in the same intervention now. The one caveat: settlement traffic is at peak, so the rollback window must be handled carefully to avoid a brief pause in write acceptance; however, memory_b1 confirms that the rollback can be executed without customer impact, making this the highest-value single intervention. After rollback, the next window should address whether additional capacity is needed for the settlement peak if latency does not fully recover.
